The refactor compiles cleanly — the Spring context wired the new `EmailNormalizer` component (had it not, startup would have failed rather than reaching the assertion). The suite is in **exactly** its baseline state: one failure, the pre-existing `coreRejectsDuplicateEmail`, still 201-vs-409.

## What I did

I prepared the ground without implementing the change. The restructuring is a single, behavior-preserving extraction:

**Extracted `EmailNormalizer`** (`rest/validation/EmailNormalizer.java`), a `@Component` mirroring the existing `TelephoneNormalizer` and `AddressNormalizer`. Email was the odd field out — telephone and address each had a dedicated normalizer component, but email was normalized by a private inline `normalizeEmail` in the controller. I moved that logic (null-safe `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`) verbatim into the component.

In `OwnerRestControllerV1` I:
- injected `emailNormalizer` through the constructor (alongside its two siblings),
- replaced both `normalizeEmail(...)` call sites (`addOwner`, `updateOwner`) with `emailNormalizer.normalize(...)`,
- deleted the now-unused private method and its javadoc.

## Why this makes the change land naturally

The upcoming duplicate-email check will be a straight mirror of `rejectDuplicateTelephone`: that method canonicalizes each existing owner via `telephoneNormalizer.canonicalize(...)` and compares through the existing `existingOwnerMatches(...)` helper. After this refactor, `rejectDuplicateEmail` can do the identical thing via `emailNormalizer.normalize(...)` — email now has the same canonical-form home its siblings have, instead of forcing the new check to reach for a private controller method or re-inline the lower-casing. The exception class + advice handler are already trivially patterned after `DuplicateOwnerTelephoneException`, so nothing there needed preparing.

## On the test state (worth being explicit)

The repo's **only** test, `coreRejectsDuplicateEmail`, is the acceptance test for the *upcoming* feature and was already failing before I touched anything (201 instead of 409). I could only make it green by implementing the duplicate-email rejection — which the task explicitly defers. My change preserves behavior exactly, so it remains at the identical failure: no currently-passing test was broken, no new failure or compile error introduced. It will go green when the actual change lands on top of this structure.
